name: Chiffon-Spire
geological_features: Towering penitente ice formations up to 500 meters tall
Nitrogen frost deposits in permanent shadow
specific_features: Enormous ice penitentes resembling draped chiffon fabric
Wind-carved ice arches and bridges between spires
description: Chiffon-Spire is an ice world dominated by penitente formations of extraordinary scale. Penitentes—blade-shaped ice pillars formed by differential sublimation—typically grow to no more than a few meters on Earth, but Chiffon-Spire's combination of intense but distant stellar radiation, thin atmosphere, and low gravity has allowed them to reach heights of five hundred meters. These towering ice blades are thin and translucent, their surfaces carved by wind into flowing curves that resemble chiffon fabric draped over invisible frameworks. They cover the planet's sunlit hemisphere in dense forests of frozen drapery.

The thin atmosphere carries barely enough gas to produce wind, but what wind exists channels between the spires with amplified force, further sculpting their surfaces and occasionally carving arches and bridges between adjacent blades. The soundscape within the spire forests is a complex mix of wind tones and the occasional crystalline crack as ice structures stress and fracture. Temperatures are deeply cold, but the translucent ice captures and redistributes stellar light in ways that create warm-toned illumination even in the shadows, the spires glowing faintly from within.

The dark hemisphere, receiving no direct light, is a different world entirely. Here the penitentes are absent, replaced by flat nitrogen frost deposits that accumulate in the permanent shadow. The boundary between the spire forests and the frost plains is a sharp line that follows the terminator, a dramatic transition from vertical complexity to horizontal flatness that circles the planet. As the planet's axial tilt shifts this boundary over its long year, old spires in newly shadowed zones gradually collapse while new ones grow in newly illuminated areas, a slow-motion forest migration tracking the light.

Chiffon-Spire's penitente formations are the largest and most dramatic known examples of the phenomenon, and they provide a natural laboratory for studying ice sublimation physics at scales impossible to replicate in any laboratory. The formations also possess an austere beauty that has attracted attention from artists and documentarians, who have produced imagery of the spire forests that has become iconic in popular media. Access is limited by the planet's remoteness and the fragility of the formations—the vibration from a landing vessel can shatter spires hundreds of meters away. Chiffon-Spire is best admired from a respectful distance, a gallery of frozen fabric that asks only to be left alone with its light.
